title: CCTC AMP students present designs - Rashad Wilson's winning design adorns dartboard cabinet project
content:
CCTC AMP students present designs - Rashad Wilson's winning design adorns dartboard cabinet project

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1A | Section: News 
 
 458
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY - The seventh cohort of Advanced Manufacturing Program students at Caroline Career and Technology Center recently presented design ideas for their current project, a dartboard cabinet.The winning design was created by Rashad Wilson, and was inspired by the doors one might find hanging in a saloon in the Old West."Rashad's dartboard design offers a new challenge for the class and me," teacher Keith Hale said.Although the students possessed the software and the capability to machine a three-dimensional object like the steer skull and horns, they had never attempted it before. "This design is more challenging than designs created by previous classes," he said.This particular project was generated three years ago when an AMP student approached Hale with the idea of manufacturing dartboard cabinets. Hale and the class were excited to make this idea a reality.Since then, AMP cabinets with dartboard with darts included have been one of AMP's most popular products, selling out even before they were presented.Each time AMP students manufacture a product, they follow the same template.It begins with research, mood-boarding and a product pitch. With dartboards, students research the history, rules and professional leagues in the game of darts. Then each student must come up with a design for the project, followed by drafting their design and placing it on a Mood Board.This Mood Board becomes a visual they can refer to as they present their product pitch.Business partners, school officials, parents and former students are then invited to watch the students' product pitches Oct. 26.One by one, students manage the difficult task of individually pitching the details and merits of their designs to the class and guests in attendance.At the end of the presentations, everyone votes and a design is chosen.The next step in the process is called "napkin sketching," which is a sketch of the product views and dimensions.These sketches are then taken to the computer aided drafting lab, where more accurate prints are made. From those prints, numeric commands are created that will drive a computer numeric control machine, which is a robot programmed to cut pieces out of stock material.Once complete, an audience is once again assembled for student presentations of the finished products, which are also offered for sale.

title: Apprenticeships explored at local high schools
author: Laura Tayman; tayman@chespub.com
content:
Apprenticeships explored at local high schools

 November 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; tayman@chespub.com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While high school students are still tasked with learning English, math, history, and science, career apprenticeships are being revitalized in Queen Anne's County and across the country, educating future workers and preparing them with marketable skills sought in high-demand industries.Karen Hesson of Kent Island High School and Betsy Ricketts of Queen Anne's County High School are in their first year serving as their school's Career Coach for students, a new position the county created this year."There is so much information available for students now, and it is hard for them and their families to navigate through it," said Hesson. "We help students identify what interests them and how to get to where they need to be to meet their goals, whether it is college, trade schools, or working directly with businesses to allow students to learn on the job." Hesson and Ricketts worked together on securing a week's worth of visitors available to meet with students during a part of their lunchtime. From military and law enforcement to county government and local businesses who are needing workers with specific skills, all were on hand to answer questions and discuss options for the future.One of the presenters was Connie Dean, the Career Technology Liaison for the Queen Anne's County Economic & Tourism Development department. Dean is assisting the two schools with finding businesses who are interested in the apprenticeship program."Students are first given skills that would be required to work in a certain business field," said Dean. Then the students work 450 hours at a partnering business to earn their official apprenticeship recognition."I try to tell businesses internships are a bigger commitment, when the apprenticeship program would be appropriate for future workers in their field," she said.Currently, there are three Kent Island students who were trained in the culinary department at Chesapeake College this semester.Aly Swann said she learned about the basics like cutting meat, how to work with knives and other kitchen tools, and how to make sauces. "I know now 100% that this is what I want to do for a living," she said.James Smith said the school was really helpful in letting him work some during the school day. "I appreciate that I got a pathway for my career. I have learned skills I will use for a long time," said Smith.Last Tuesday, was military and law enforcement day for the Queen Anne's apprentice week, with recruiters from all armed forces branches, answering questions about basic training, money for college, and traveling the globe.Troopers Christopher Bekefiand Doug Prince provided information on the Maryland State Police Cadet program, where students aged 17-19 are assigned to perform duties that do not require police authority (example helping with crowds at large public events). Cadets are also assigned to work under the supervision of a Trooper at a truck inspection station or on patrol.They also have an explorer program for students aged 14-18, where they are introduced to various divisions and tactics like crime scene investigations, traffic stops, and forensics.Adam Tolley, supervisor of Career and Technology Education for Queen Anne's Public Schools, was pleased to see so many students engaging with a variety of workforce representatives. "This is a very organized way to provide students who are beginning to think about real career options," he said.County Commissioner Philip Dumenil was present to view the new apprentice week program first hand at Queen Anne's High School. "I like new opportunities for exposure to these kind of programs," said Dumenil. "Lots of money can still be made in the trade fields. Not every kid wants to go to college." Queen Anne's student Austin Hahn, just a sophomore, has already chosen a career for his future, and that, said Ricketts, makes him a perfect apprentice candidate.Hahn has chosen to pursue a career in marine mechanics and pipe welding and wishes to move to the Gulf of Mexico in Louisiana or Texas where he has family. "My grandfather taught me a lot about it," said Hahn. "He said it would be the best money I could ever make. When he passed away, I knew I would definitely do it."

title: Caroline Commissioners approve summer school grant
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Caroline Commissioners approve summer school grant

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 17 | Section: News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - After expressing appreciation for the contributions of public health professionals, the Caroline County Commission held about an hour-long meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Nov. 21.Jamie Beachy, director of Caroline County Recreation and Parks, presented a grant award from the Maryland Department of Education to fund Caroline County summer learning centers.The commissioners accepted the three-year $1.2 million grant."What this means for the first summer year is that we will be looking at five school sites, and unlike our previous years that we targeted 700 students, we will be targeting 1,100 for next summer," Beachy said. "Yes, we are insane. We're fully aware that that's going to be a very big lift for us." Beachy said that for the two years following 2024, "without another funding stream becoming available, we will drop back down to three elementary schools with a total of 400 students." In other business, the commissioners approved a $1,011,834 contract with Nashville-based Wellpath LLC to provide medical services for inmates at the county jail.Two surplus vehicles will be offered for sale, deemed by the County Commissioners to be "no longer needed, outdated, unsafe, or (their) condition has deteriorated to the point that maintenance costs exceeds its practical value." A 2012 Dodge ambulance with 211,797 miles and a 2014 Dodge Ram with 218,742 miles will be auctioned locally.Ryan White has left his position as director of the Department of Public Works, and that position may be reconfigured before it is advertised.Commission Vice President Larry Porter expressed some concern about "the scope of what is going to be able to be done by public works." "At some point, in my opinion, (it's) going to have to be reduced. There's going to have to be more things contracted out," Porter said.Commission President Travis Breeding said, "I've been giving this position a lot of thought, and I think it would be helpful to have someone there who is wellversed in the design process, permitting process, bid process.I almost feel like it's a two-person role." title: School principals prepare for the Blueprint For Maryland's Future
author: Cait Kelley And Caley Fox Shannon
content:
School principals prepare for the Blueprint For Maryland's Future

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Cait Kelley And Caley Fox Shannon | Page: 12 | Section: News 
 
 777
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OCEAN CITY - As Maryland rolls out the 2021 landmark education reform law called the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, many school administrators are unsure what the plan means for their schools.At the annual School Leaders Conference held Nov. 2-4 in Ocean City, state officials and school principals reviewed the details of the Blueprint and discussed how it will be implemented in each school district.The wave of impending policy changes are meant to address the challenges facing educators and students across the state.The Blueprint is grounded in the analysis of a group of independent policy experts formed by the state in 2016 to establish a baseline for education reform.The group was commonly referred to as the Kirwan Commission after its chair, William E. Kirwan, chancellor emeritus of the University System of Maryland.By 2019, the Kirwan Commission had come to some sobering conclusions about Maryland's education system.Half of all teachers leave the profession within the first five years. Only two out of every five kindergarteners arrive in the classroom ready to learn. And just a third of students leave high school being "college and career ready" in English and math."That was pre-pandemic.So generally speaking, it's gotten worse," said Rachel Hise, a policy specialist who worked for the state in tandem with the Kirwan Commission.Explaining the commission's findings to school leaders in Ocean City, she said the independent body concluded that "ultimately, the status quo is unsustainable."The Maryland General Assembly passed the Blueprint for Maryland's Future in February 2021, overriding a veto by then-Gov.Larry Hogan, a Republican who had cost concerns about the plan.The Blueprint allocates $3.8 billion to schools over the next 10 years.Hise is now executive director of the Blueprint's Accountability and Implementation Board. She said the policy changes will make sure students are ready to learn in kindergarten and ready to succeed when they graduate high school.Because public schools lack the capacity to fulfill this mandate alone, the state will fund programming via private pre-K providers as well."The goal is a socioeconomically integrated pre-K system that is publicly funded, but that is provided by both public schools and private providers," Hise told administrators in Ocean City.The Blueprint will also mean big changes in high schools."What the Blueprint really envisions is we want kids to be college and career ready by 10th grade, so that the second two years of high school students can focus on the pathway that they're interested in pursuing," Hise said.The Blueprint aims to meet this goal through curriculum changes in English and math in addition to apprenticeships and technical education programs.Implementing the Blueprint at the school level falls squarely on school administrators, said Addie Kaufman, executive director of the Maryland Association of Secondary School Principals."There was no doubt that the Blueprint would be a part of this conference, and the understanding of the Blueprint is actually key," she said in an interview.After learning more about the Blueprint at the conference, some principals said they are hopeful that the reforms will address their schools' priorities.Teachers are struggling to make do with salaries in the current economy, said Principal Ryan Daniel of Fort Foote Elementary in Prince George's County."I know a lot of my teachers have to have after-school jobs or second jobs to compensate for their salary," she said.The Blueprint will raise the minimum salary for teachers to $60,000 across the state by 2026. And if teachers obtain National Board Certification, the Blueprint allows them to earn up to an additional $17,000 per year.Other schools have yet to feel the concrete impact of the Blueprint."Honestly, I'm still reading and learning, and I think that they're doing a really slow roll out intentionally for us, which is good," said Jamie Miller, the principal at Broadneck Elementary in Arnold. "We have people at the board level who are becoming sort of experts and then they're going to disseminate to us."Miller expressed a mix of excitement about the expansion of pre-K and trepidation about her school's capacity to meet the need.In March 2023, every school district submitted a detailed plan to the Accountability and Implementation Board for rolling out the Blueprint in their schools."The plans are fine, but they really are a baseline," Hise said. "There's a need for more innovative thinking."The Accountability and Implementation Board expects updated plans from every district in March 2024, and has offered every district a $100,000 grant to hire a strategic planning expert. All but Frederick and Worcester counties took the state up on that deal.

 DENTON - Caroline County Public Schools sophomores explored career options at the Denton Rotary's 2023 Youth Career Exploration Fair Nov. 21 at the General James F. Fretterd Community Center.A number of Caroline County Public School sophomores had the opportunity to visit with representatives from a variety of businesses and attend workshops to help them explore career possibilities before they graduate from high school.Hosted by the Rotary Club of Denton, the 10th Grade Career Exploration Fair was sponsored by Smiles by Holsinger, Shore United Bank, Summit Community Bank and Sisk Fulfillment.The Denton Rotary has been providing this yearly event to 10th grade students since 2013; however, the COVID pandemic temporarily suspended it."The purpose of the event is to spark an interest and open up career possibilities to our 10th graders so they can be career ready when they graduate," said Sue Simmons, a Denton Rotarian and the event chair.This year was the highest attendance ever, with 97 students from Colonial Richardson High School, North County High School and the Caroline Career and Technology Center, who were split up into groups for the day. Nearly 30 small and large businesses set up vendor exhibits.Each group was assigned to a table with a business mentor - an adult to help match them with possible careers that are compatible with their interests or expose them to new ideas and opportunities to consider.Students were encouraged to explore careers that match their personal interests, such as working outside, being a problem solver, caring for others or owning their own business.Each student also attended two of the four workshops that were offered. Workshops included "Unlocking Your Potential at Chesapeake College" by Marci Leach, director of program development at Chesapeake Community College, and J.P. Kelly, business and industry navigator at Chesapeake Community College; "Mental Health Means Inner Wealth" by Sara Porter-Lepore, LCSW-C, and Cara Calloway, mental health coordinator for CCPS; "How To Rock a Job Interview" by Deborah Boulden, youth outreach coordinator for the Upper Shore Workforce Investment Board; and "Way to Be: Exploring Career Interests" by Abigail Trice, Next Generation Scholars coordinator for Caroline County.Participating students also had the opportunity to meet students from other schools, as each group was pre-assigned to their tables by Lindsey McCormick, CCPS director of college and career.Ten juniors who attended the fair last year returned as mentors to help guide the sophomores through the day.A bonus to the program was a special visit from Devon Beck, an NCHS graduate, songwriter, hip hop artist, podcaster and Talbot County Public Schools Equity Facilitator. Beck shared with the students his own story and provided a positive message about being true to themselves and finding a career that is meaningful to them.The Rotary Club of Denton thanked Dr. Derek Simmons, McCormick and Robert Gowen from the CCPS Board of Education; Eric Cook, Ann Ferkler, and Brad Plutschak from CCPS; as well as table mentors Danielle Forrest of Shore United, Linda Prochaska of Appleseed Books, Victor Reynolds of CASA of Caroline, Richard Warfield of the Caroline Review, Esther Curtis of SUN Behavioral Health), Desiree Jefferson and America McKinney of His Hope Ministries, Kristi English of APG Media Chesapeake, Angel Perez of the Caroline Culinary Arts Center, Kat Stork of Shore Strategies LLC, and Sarah Kilmon of Talbot County Communications.

title: Superintendent Outlines Budget Priorities, Timeline
author: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com
content:
Superintendent Outlines Budget Priorities, Timeline

 December 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; Cconnolly@Chespub.Com | Page: 15 | Section: News 
 
 785
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - The conundrum of uncertain Blueprint demands coupled with a projected decrease in pandemic-related grant funding for Caroline County Public Schools is proving to be a challenge for Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons, school administrators and district staff as they build a budget for fiscal year 2025.And because the dilemma impacts the traditional budgeting timeline employed in previous years, at the Dec. 5 meeting of the Caroline County Board of Education, the Superintendent Simmons received more time to develop a more realistic budget.
The Board of Education approved Simmons's request to revise the traditional timeline and move his final budget proposal from February to April.
"We do not have a good idea of what state revenues look like until the General Assembly gets done doing their work, which is April," Simmons said.
While some demands of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a set of policies and spending for education in the state's public schools, are clear, others are still being modified. The "uncertainties" of the unfunded legislative mandate have created budgetary challenges for school administrators across the state.
One of the demands for school districts is funding dual enrollment for high school students who wish to take college courses. Blueprint's College and Career Readiness standards require school districts to pay for any student who meets the minimum requirements for dual enrollment. At roughly $1,000 per student per semester, CCPS spent $130,000 in 2023 for juniors and seniors to take courses at Chesapeake College. While "it's great for the kids," Simmons said, the Blueprint requirement presents a budget challenge.
Another "cost of doing Blueprint business" is meeting the mandated starting teacher salary of $60,000 by fiscal year 2027.
Grant funding "is kind of how Caroline County has survived," Simmons said.
But some of that funding will decrease or cease altogether in 2024.
Both American Rescue Plan and Maryland Leads grant funding will sunset in Sept. 2024. In addition, the funding formula for Blueprint shows a 1.7% increase in state funding from last year, the lowest per year increase in the formula, Simmons said.
The CCPS budget, typical of school systems across the state is 80% people, Simmons said.
"The rule of thumb is anywhere between 80% to 90% of your budget is people, and when you take people out and you take out paying for your electric and your fuel and heating your buildings and running your buses and those sorts of things, you're probably left with somewhere between the neighborhood of 5% to 7% every year that truly is discretionary," Simmons said.
And while "about 14% of our money comes from the county government, the rest of it comes from state and federal, which is also why those numbers are important," he said.
Most categories in Blueprint require financing at the school level, adding additional elements of complexity and compliance, and requiring full time accounting level position, Simmons said.
Besides Blueprint's requirements, budget pressures also include the rate of inflation at over 3.5%, multiyear contracts that will come up for renewal in 2024 that will likely be higher than the rate of inflation and global issues impacting the cost of goods, including fuel.
However, the budgeting challenge is not "all doom and gloom," Simmons said.
Caroline County has schools that qualify for "concentration of poverty" grant funding. While the funding is restricted to individual schools and can't support programs or positions at the district level, it helps take some pressure off the district to fund, for example, an afterschool program or reading intervention at a specific school.
Federalsburg and Greensboro elementary schools already qualify; Colonel Richardson Middle School received its first concentration of poverty grant in 2023.
"It's likely we will see multiple other schools added as the Free and Reduced Meals rates maintain or increase," Simmons said. Because the concentration of poverty funding formula relies on Free and Reduced Meals data, Simmons said, "I feel very confident all nine of our schools will get there."
As for the budgeting process, Simmons and his team will continue to work on the budget, try to find funding sources and work with the County finance office into 2024. Negotiating with the teachers' association will play a role, as well as a joint budget meeting with the Caroline County Commissioners.
"We also have a very good working relationship with the county commissioners," Simmons said. "We are not one of those counties that walks over to the county commissioners and drops an additional increase of $3, 4 or 5 million on them." The final CCPS budget is due to the county commissioners by the end of June.
Priorities in the fiscal year 2025 CCPS budget are competitive salaries and benefits for all employees, maintaining reasonable staffing levels across the district, maintaining high yield positions and programs that were included in pandemic-related grants and implementing the Blueprint as required.

title: Tcps Gives Update On Its Priorities At Board Meeting
author: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub. Com
content:
Tcps Gives Update On Its Priorities At Board Meeting

 December 15, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato; Mtrovato@Chespub. Com | Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 937
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - At a Talbot County Board of Education meeting Wednesday, administrators gave an update on the school system's priorities.Talbot County Public Schools' three priorities, identified in the spring, are academic equity and achievement, fostering an engaging environment and hiring and retaining highly qualified and diverse staff.
Since sharing the priorities with the entire school system in August, Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi said they have been working to "infuse" the priorities everywhere.
"In my roundtables, out in the community, in schools," she said. "We're constantly talking about those three priorities."
At the meeting, strategies and metrics associated with each priority were shared.
ACADEMIC EQUITY AND ACHIEVEMENT When it comes to academic equity and achievement, TCPS has six strategies, including implementing additional interventions for students in and outside the classroom, hiring additional math coaches and implementing more assessments to measure growth.
Assistant Superintendent for Curriculum and Instruction Helga Einhorn said that since improving math was identified as a priority by the board, the district has added the NWEA MAP Growth Assessment for mathematics.
"Prior to this year, we did not have a standardized assessment that would allow us to collect this type of data as we had with reading," Einhorn said. "We felt it was important, if we were going to make changes throughout the year, to progress monitor our students throughout the year."
Students in kindergarten through fifth grade took the beginning of the year MAP Growth Assessment for mathematics.
Einhorn said teachers were impressed with how well students performed.
Overall, 14% of those students were in the 80th percentile or higher, 19% were between the 61st and 80th percentile, 18% were between the 41st and 60th percentile, 21% were between the 21st and 40th percentile and 25% were between the 1st and 20th percentile.
Along with measuring growth through testing throughout the year, Einhorn said teachers are working very closely with the K-6 Math Curriculum Supervisor Daisy Bradwell.
"They are doing a deep dive into the curriculum," Einhorn said, adding that Bradwell is working with teachers to identify what things might be missing from the curriculum.
FOSTERING AN ENGAGING ENVIRONMENT Director of Student Services Darlene Spurrier started off her presentation by listing different strategies the district is employing to achieve fostering an engaging environment.
These strategies include school-based mental health services and substance abuse intervention and prevention; restorative practices training; and individual school wellness plans and wellness coaches.
"Many of (these strategies) are ongoing and will not ever really move to completed because they're things that we're just going to continue to do," she said.
When it came to data, Spurrier shared the results of three climate surveys - an internal survey from this year and the Maryland School Climate Surveys from last year and the year before that. Each of the surveys measure student and educator attitudes on four domains: community, environment, relationships and safety.
Comparing the student survey TCPS took this year to the state's survey from last year, within those four domains, students considered physical safety, physical environment and participation and engagement significantly better this year than the previous two years.
Comparing the teacher survey TCPS took this year to the state's survey from last year, teachers also ranked participation and engagement and physical safety significantly higher. They also ranked substance abuse higher than last year, meaning it is less of a concern in schools this year. Teachers ranked bullying lower on the scale this year compared to last year, meaning it is more of a concern.
HIGHLY QUALIFIED AND DIVERSE STAFF Assistant Superintendent for Administrative and Support Services Lynne Duncan presented data on new hires, recruitment and TCPS's Grow Your Own Teachers Scholarship Program.
Before she spoke, Pepukayi said that retaining, not just recruiting, is important to the district.
"With the shortages across our nation in education, we want to make sure the people who are here, we're tending to," she said.
According to Duncan's presentation, last school year, 197 out of 234 people, or 84%, accepted offers of employment.
This year, 90 out of 126 people, or 71%, accepted offers of employment.
Duncan said that, to date, four of those new hires this year have left employment.
In terms of demographics of new teaching staff this year, 32 teachers are white and two are Hawaiian.
TCPS attended seven recruitment fairs last school year. Duncan said it yielded one support staff employee.
The district plans to attend a total of eight recruiting events this school year. So far, it has visited three.
Of the five people enrolled in the district's Grow Your Own Teachers Scholarship Program last year, four have been hired. The program gives TCPS students enrolled in college a scholarship if they agree to teach in the district after they graduate. Duncan said that of the nine remaining students enrolled in the program, one will graduate this month, one will graduate in June of 2024, three will graduate in 2026 and four will graduate in 2027.
At the end of the meeting, board member Jymil Thompson said he could see that the administrative team has clear vision, alignment and transparency.
"I think you all do a fabulous, fabulous job of that," he said. "I want to see where the district's going to be in a couple years because I think it's definitely trickling in the right direction. So I'm anxious to be a part of that."

 EASTON - Easton High School senior William O'Donnell has been chosen to represent Talbot County in the Maryland General Assembly Student Page Program for the 2024 Legislative Session.In 2022, former Gov. Larry Hogan appointed O'Donnell to serve on the Maryland Youth Advisory Council, where he is vice chair.
He holds several additional leadership positions, including president of the Maryland Junior Classical League, Shore-Rivers Upper Shore Youth Environmental Action Summit leader and Eastern Shore divisional liaison of the Maryland Association of Student Councils.
O'Donnell is co-president of the Easton High Interact Club and vice president of the Latin Honor Society.
O'Donnell also participates in Talbot County Teen Court, Latin Academic Olympics, speech and debate, National Honor Society and rowing. He interns with Talbot County Democrats, helps educate elementary students about STEM and has represented Maryland at the National Junior Classical League convention.
The Maryland Association of Secondary School Principals acknowledged O'Donnell for being one of the first students to present at an principals' conference.
His group presentations on artificial intelligence in education and the panel on school safety motivated the association to allow student presentations at all future events.
O'Donnell has received several awards, including recognition as an Advanced Placement Scholar with honors, the 2023 National Latin Exam Magna Cum Laude medal, and the Maryland Association of Student Councils Certified Workshop Presenter status.
Maryland high school seniors have served as student pages for members of the state legislature since 1970.
Each year, 105 pages and 36 alternates from across Maryland are selected by their local school systems to represent their schools and counties.
Selected pages serve two nonconsecutive weeks in either the Senate or House of Delegates.
During the 13 weeks of session, which run from the second week in January to early April, each page serves one week during the first seven weeks and returns for a second week during the last six. The duties of pages are driven by the schedule of the chamber to which they are assigned.
Requirements include being a high school senior who is at least 16 years of age, residing and attending a public or nonpublic high school in Maryland and having an interest in government and history.
Interested students should apply through their schools in September and selection is completed by Oct. 1 of each year. More information about the Maryland General Assembly Page Program is available at dls.maryland.gov/careers/student-page-program.

 CHESTERTOWN - Plastic rings and bean bags were tossed, kids did crafts and Santa was on hand for the annual Sensory Holiday Celebration dedicated to children who receive special education services.Held at the Kent County Middle School on Wednesday, it's in its sixth year, organized by the Kent County Infants and Toddlers program.
It's a Christmas party, just on a smaller scale, sensitive to children with disabilities such as autism.
Reason being, overstimulation is a common experience for individuals with autism.
It was a fun time with friends and family. Kids made ice cream cones or enjoyed hot chocolate with their parents.
The children were happy to get a bag of Christmas items to take home. All of them were gifted with a "Nice List Certification" directly from the desk of Santa Claus.

Parents and friends interacted with professionals in the field over pizza, cookies and tiny juice boxes.
Elizabeth Tussing the Family Resource Center's parent coordinator and organizer said, "This year we have Santa, and it's good because kids can receive individualized time with him. It's not a long line so they don't feel the pressure." Also in attendance were staff from all three Judy Centers in Kent County: Rock Hall, Chestertown and the newest, Galena.
Professionals from the Family Resource Center and Special Education Citizens Advisory Committee, (SECAC) were there, helping with the event and being a positive presence.
For those in the community interested, SECAC meets on the fourth Wednesday of each month at the Kent County Middle School.
On Jan. 24, starting at 5 p.m, Parents Place of Maryland will teach on the transition process for student's Individualized Educational Plans.

title: Character Counts - Queen Anne's County commissioners recognize Gavin Schulte
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com
content:
Character Counts - Queen Anne's County commissioners recognize Gavin Schulte

 January 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com | Page: 7 | Section: News 
 
 559

 STEVENSVILLE - Recently, the Queen Anne's County Commissioners recognized Kent Island High School junior Gavin Schulte for their Character Counts Spotlight on Caring."The holiday season is a great way to to show those around us that we care," Commissioner Philip L. Dumenil said.
"Caring for others is a great way to show good character."
Schulte is the son of Kent Island High School art teacher and the Queen Anne's County Teacher of the Year for 2023, Andrea Schulte, and Brendan Schulte, coach and Health and Fitness for Life teacher, also at Kent Island High School.
He is a member of the school's Unified baseball and weightlifting activities.
Dumenil said Schulte began showing caring at an early age, starting when he was a student at Matapeake Elementary School.
He would routinely organize coat drives in the fall for the Knights of Columbus and peanut butter and jelly and cereal drives to support summer backpack programs. Additionally, he helps and supports serving 1,200 meals the day before Thanksgiving.
According to Jone Taylor of Queen Anne's County Social Services, Schulte, who had known Taylor through being on a baseball team with her son, reached out to her in 2019.
He was concerned for foster children who came into care of the Department of Social Services.
"He started putting together duffel bags filled with special items to help a child feel a little more at ease, and give them hope that they are safe, and someone cares for them," said Taylor.
The bags were packed with items such as a blanket, a book, a night light, toothbrush and other toiletries, as well as a stuffed animal.
"Gavin didn't just throw things together at random. He took the time to make bags for children of all ages, and made sure to mark them by age and gender," Taylor said.
Taylor said Schulte asked her a lot of questions, wanting to understand what happens when a child comes into care.
She believed he understood that sometimes a caseworker has to bring a child or children to safety in the middle of the night.
"Being able to quickly grab a bag for the child helps ease a little of the anxiety they might be feeling," said Taylor.
"Gavin took the time to listen to what was needed."
Schulte even provided diaper bags filled with items for newborns with a variety of diaper sizes and gender neutral items, including receiving blankets, a bottle, pacifiers, wipes, diapers and diaper cream.
Schulte builds an Amazon Wish List and purchases items with his own money if necessary.
Taylor said Schulte checks in with her every four to five months to see what the department is running low on, or if they have other needs.
"Last year we talked about children needing socks," said Taylor. "A few days later, he dropped off bags with over 40 pairs of brand new socks of various sizes and colors."
Taylor said she was impressed with this young man and appreciates the heart he has for helping others.
"Gavin has truly been a blessing to children in need in Queen Anne's County," she said. "He never looks for accolades or praise, but when I think of someone who is the epitome of selfless giving, that would be Gavin."
Commissioner Dumenil agreed. "I know this young man," he said. "He is such a great kid."

title: Problems persist in juvenile services schooling
author: Steph Quinn; Capital News Service
content:
Problems persist in juvenile services schooling

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Steph Quinn; Capital News Service | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 569
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SABILLASVILLE - The graduate's mom, peers and teachers knew he was going to reach his goal, though his principal, Todd Rasher, said the other students incarcerated at the Victor Cullen Center in rural northern Frederick County didn't see "all the footwork" it took to earn his GED."This diploma ain't really too much because I knew that I was going to get it," the 17-year-old said to his graduation audience on Oct. 18, wearing a cap and gown, kente stole and black wristband adorned with, "Don't give up." The graduate, whose identity CNS is shielding because he is a minor, was charged as an adult before his case was transferred to juvenile court.
Rasher said he passed the tests necessary to earn his GED on the first try, inspiring his fellow students to take the tests themselves.
Not all incarcerated young people are able to continue their education, much less attain a degree. Two years after the Maryland General Assembly transferred responsibility for incarcerated students' education from the state Education Department to an independent school board within the Juvenile Services Department, students confined in Maryland's secure youth facilities continue to face multiple long-standing challenges, according to experts and state audit reports.
Teacher vacancy rates of 30% in the most populous Juvenile Services schools have led to reliance on streaming instruction in subjects such as math and science.
David Domenici, director of education and senior adviser to the Juvenile Services secretary, said streaming instruction is "not ideal" for the "vast majority" of students but better than packets of photocopied activities.
Juvenile Services teacher vacancies have persisted through tensions between Maryland's education and Juvenile Services agencies over the past decade about who bears responsibility for educating incarcerated young people and how best to do so. Those vacancies continue through teachers' lack of summer and winter breaks and low pay relative to teachers employed by local school districts.
Bills seeking pay parity and summer breaks for juvenile services teachers failed in 2016, 2019 and 2020, often pitting experts from Education and Juvenile Services against each other. The General Assembly established a statewide education board within Juvenile Services in 2021 in response to monitors' and advocacy groups' repeated findings of high staff turnover and vacancies, inadequate services for learning disabled students and a lack of support for students returning to community schools.
But the law did not require pay parity or align facilities' teaching calendar more closely with local schools.
But lost instructional time is greatest due to a lack of residential advisers, according to audits of Juvenile Services schools by the state Office of the Inspector General.
Departmental policy requires that residential staff escort students from their living units to classrooms while maintaining a minimum staff-to-youth ratio. When there aren't enough residential staff, students don't move.
Students were late to class 203 times across Juvenile Services facilities due to residential staff shortages between April and June alone, according to the audits. Teachers had to teach class inside the living units 43 times in the 90-day inspection period.
Getting students in the classroom, even if they are late, Domenici said, is better than class on the living units.
The department is working toward a goal of 90% on-time attendance in school by shifting all onsite adults to escort students to school, he said.

title: 'Diving Deep' with dyslexia: Local special education teacher works to raise awareness
author: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat
content:
'Diving Deep' with dyslexia: Local special education teacher works to raise awareness

 January 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TAMARA FORTE Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 1217
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — What do Robin Williams, Jay Leno, Albert Einstein, Alexander Graham Bell, Magic Johnson, Jennifer Aniston, Gwen Stefani, Abraham Lincoln, and Arnold Schwarzenegger all have in common? They all have dyslexia.Lindsey Parte, a mother of two boys and Special Education teacher, has reignited the Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter that fizzled out during the Covid pandemic.
Parte shares that she has been "diving deep into advocating and teaching herself (about dyslexia)" for the last three years.
When Parte's older son, Lincoln, was six years old, he struggled with both speech and reading. Parte said a red flag to her son's learning struggle was "knowing how smart he was but not understanding why reading was so hard."
Parte explains that her two-year younger son was making gains on her older son. In contrast, reading was coming with ease to her younger son.
On the first day of second grade, Lincoln (her older son) came home and said, "I can't do this. I can't read. I hate school." Lincoln was frustrated with learning and wanted to quit.
It was heartbreaking for Parte as a mother and as a special education teacher herself as no one wants to see their child struggle, especially with learning. Parte explained, reading is the gateway to learning and lifelong success, and as such, learning to read successfully is vital to all.
Two years after Parte first suspected Lincoln was dyslexic, Lincoln got his formal diagnosis. Parte explained that getting the diagnosis meant freedom for her and her son.
She recounts, "I will never forget the utter sigh of relief when we told him he has dyslexia. It all made sense to him from that moment on. Within a week, he was already talking about it in class and advocating for himself. And most importantly, we got our boy back. His light turned back on."
According to the Mayo Clinic, dyslexia is "a learning disorder that involves difficulty reading due to problems identifying speech sounds and learning how they relate to letters and words (decoding). Also called a reading disability, dyslexia is a result of individual differences in areas of the brain that process language."
An MRI shows the physical differences in the brain composition of a dyslexic thinker versus a non-dyslexic thinker. Dyslexia is so common that one in five people are a dyslexic learners.
What is it like to have dyslexia? How can I help and support a dyslexic learner? What are the early indicators of dyslexia? These questions and many others will be answered at 6:30 p.m., Feb. 20, at the "Experience Dyslexia: A Dyslexia Simulation" workshop at the Queen Anne's County Library Kent Island Branch location.
The free event, hosted by Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter, aims to raise dyslexia awareness, empower families to support their children, encourage educational interventions, and ultimately influence policy makers to support Maryland students with dyslexia.
All are welcome. The event will offer six stations to help understand the dyslexic learner: Learn to Read, Listen to Me, Write with Mirrors, Name the Letter, Write or Left, and Unfair Hearing Test.
Parte says,"The two biggest takeaways I have learned over the last year of my deep dive into my son's brain and the way he learns are early identification is crucial (as young as five-years-old); and the dyslexic brain requires instruction to be explicit, systematic, cumulative and multisensory.
"It should integrate the teaching of listening, speaking, reading, spelling, vocabulary, fluency, handwriting and written expression. There should be an emphasis on the structure of language: phonology, orthography, morphology, syntax and semantics. Training teachers and educating parents is also of the utmost importance," she continued.
Since then, Lincoln has helped his mom set up and lead workshops. In October, to celebrate Dyslexia Awareness Month, this mother and son duo led the Halloween-themed workshop entitled "There is nothing scarier than not being able to read."
Parte believes in dyslexia awareness and education with her whole being, which is why she fundraised, on her own, to purchase the upcoming workshop materials.
After more than three years of advocating, Parte promotes all adults to learn as much as they can by listening to podcasts, attending free trainings, reading books and fact sheets, and much more.
Moving forward, what steps can we take?
"Release the stigma. Embrace the label," Parte said. "The label means freedom. It gives a child the right to read. The right to appropriate instruction which in turns means success in reading and regaining self confidence. We got our child back the moment we told him he had dyslexia. The label opens a world of resources for your child to feel good about themselves. Priority is a child's mental and social wellbeing."
Dyslexic Learners have many strengths and show a lot of leadership skills. Some other positive skills of dyslexic learners include: problem-solving, big picture thinking, creativity, empathetic, and entrepreneurial skills.
Parte shared things parents can do to help their struggling reader if they suspect their child has dyslexia:
Testing is everything. You will be surprised how relieved your child is with a "diagnosis".
Finding the right intervention specialist (tutors in reading are not the same as someone trained and certified in structured reading interventions like Orton Gillingham). Tutoring at least three times a week is most effective. The key to remediation is "go as fast as you can and as slow as you need to". Early intervention is crucial especially to maintain your child's confidence in school.
Deep dive in your own research. It will help with advocacy, ensuring the right assessments are being used, and knowing the right questions to vet organizations and other folks who claim to want to help your student.
Read to your child not so they learn to read but so that they develop their reading comprehension and vocabulary while they are learning to read with appropriate interventions.
If your child receives the diagnosis of dyslexia, tell them, she encourages. Share all the amazing qualities a dyslexic thinker has and famous people who have dyslexia. Show them a photograph of a dyslexic brain vs typical brain.
Knowledge and support in this process are so important. You don't have to go through this emotional journey alone. Connect with your local Decoding Dyslexia chapter.
Parte explains, "Most children with dyslexia can succeed in school with tutoring or a specialized education program. Emotional support also plays an important role.
Though there's no cure for dyslexia, early assessment and intervention result in the best outcome. Sometimes dyslexia goes undiagnosed for years and isn't recognized until adulthood, but it's never too late to seek help."
Community support, awareness, education, and training will help all our learners learn in the best ways to be successful, happy learners. Together, we can impact our future and the future of our children. If you cannot attend the workshop at the library but are interested in gaining resources and learning more, you can email decodingdyslexiaES@gmail.com for more information and for a Welcome Newsletter with a list of more resources.
Currently, Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter is a grassroots movement (not a nonprofit), which means it has no funding and is paid for all out-of-pocket. It is run by parents who are also working professionals.
"The fight continues," Parte said, "Until every single child (and their families) don't have to go through this hell and back to learn how to read."
To support and make a donation to Decoding Dyslexia Maryland Eastern Shore Chapter, you can also email Parte at the email above.

title: Blueprint pillar chairs share Caroline's progress
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Blueprint pillar chairs share Caroline's progress

 January 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1301
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — At the Jan. 9 meeting of the Caroline County Board of Education, several supervisors provided updates on progress towards meeting requirements of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future, a set of policies and dedicated funding seeking to transform several aspects of the state's public education system by 2026.Assistant Superintendent Dr. Tara Downes said the district has been receiving additional guidance from the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) and Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB) since spring 2023.
As a result, required tasks have been "chunked out" over a more manageable timeline, and the pillar chairs are "actually ahead of schedule" with some aspects of the plan.
"The pillar chairs have been phenomenal in being proactive when it comes to the work," Downes said.
According to its website, "The Blueprint for Maryland's Future was passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021 to transform public education in the state into a world-class education system. The Blueprint will increase education funding by $3.8 billion each year over the next 10 years, enrich student experiences and accelerate student outcomes, as well as improve the quality of education for all children in Maryland, especially those who have been historically underserved."
"The Blueprint really involves everything that we're doing on a daily basis," said Caroline County Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons.
According to the Blueprint website, "The bold work of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future is organized into five distinct pillars." Each pillar has a set of objectives to help administrators and educators align instruction and community support to them and determine needed resources.
Pillar 1: Early Childhood Education
The main focus of Pillar 1 is the expansion of pre-kindergarten for three-year-olds and four-year-olds, said CCPS Supervisor of Instruction Elizabeth Saylor, who serves as Pillar 1 chair.
Of the 375 pre-K students enrolled as of Sept. 30, 58 are in pre-K three and 317 are in pre-K four. The main focus currently are Tier One families who are "up to 300% of the federal poverty level, or 319 students. As of Jan. 9, 395 students were enrolled in pre-K," Saylor said.
A challenge is the need for private daycare providers, who must follow Blueprint's criteria. Providing more qualified and more certified staff is another challenge both for Pillar 1 compliance and workforce development, an objective of Pillar 2.
"Making sure families and students are ready for kindergarten" is ultimately the focus of the pillar, Saylor said.
Pillar 2: High Quality and Diverse Teachers and Leaders
CCPS Supervisor of Human Resources Dr. Rob Willoughby addressed four objectives of Pillar 2, which focuses on the recruitment of high quality and diverse teachers and leaders.
Chesapeake College has been "a fantastic partner with us through the Maryland Leads" grant initiative, he said. The district recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Mount St. Mary's University, which offers a fully online bachelor's degree in elementary education.
Willoughby's group is looking at other ways of providing staff and enhancing qualifications, including encouraging National Board Certified Teacher credentialing.
Forty-eight teachers are currently in the process of pursuing that certification. "That is 10% of our teaching staff pursuing a really rigorous national certification," he said.
A Pillar 2 challenge includes a starting teacher salary of $60,000 by Blueprint's July 1, 2026, deadline.
"Our starting teacher salary this year $53,167, and … we're about $6,800 to the end," Willoughby said. "If you divide that over the three fiscal years we have, that means it needs to go up at least $2,278 (per year)."
Pillar 3: College and Career Readiness
Blueprint's third pillar focuses on students' college and career readiness.
College and Career Readiness Director Lindsey McCormick explained the progress being made towards complying with Pillar 3 of the Blueprint as the district works under interim standards. Students are assessed at the end of their 10th grade year and can choose a career pathway. The district offers 16 Career and Technology Education (CTE) pathways.
In addition to pursuing a college track and taking advanced placement courses, students can receive career counseling. Students in AP courses are now required to sit for the exams in the spring; the tests are paid for by the district.
"I am very pleased to say that this year through our MOU with the (Upper Shore) Workforce Investment Board, we have added one high school and one middle school career coach that are in the buildings five days a week working with students," McCormick said.
She said the district is growing the youth apprenticeship program and modeling it for businesses.
If students are not college and career ready, the district is working on a pilot program to provide supports, including online study, to help them meet state standards, McCormick said. Chesapeake College supplied data from the past three years that showed students' learning online was just as successful as classroom learning.
Pillar 4: More Resources to Ensure that All Students are Successful
Pillar 4 of Blueprint seeks to provide students with more resources that could help them succeed.
Supervisor of Instruction Christal Harkowa, one of the co-chairs for Pillar 4, updated the school board on multilingual learners.
The district has hired two multilingual learner family coordinators to work with Spanish- and Haitian Creole-speaking constituents.
"We have really been able to improve our communication with our families," Harkowa said. "They are very dedicated; they stay after (school), they attend all kinds of after school events, parent conferences when we need them for 504 or IEP (Individualized Education Program) meetings to make sure our parents understand what the needs of their students are and to be able to advocate and ask questions."
She said her goal by the end of this school year is to "identify MLL families for parent leadership opportunities."
To support MLLs in instruction and language acquisition, the district is providing ongoing professional development for teachers and instructional assistants while "being respectful of their planning time," Harkowa said. Another focus is helping students develop English proficiency in elementary school.
Supervisor of Special Education Erica McDonald discussed the objective of closing the achievement gap for students with disabilities.
The leadership team created a mission statement at the beginning of the current school year, provided Goalbook toolkit training and additional training to help teachers and co-teachers meet objectives and monitor "disproportionate identification and disciplinary practices."
"Our special education teacher specialists have really taken on the role of educational diagnosticians," she said.
A Blueprint objective is to "establish or enhance Community Schools in areas of concentrated poverty." Three CCPS schools — Federalsbury Elementary, Greensboro Elementary and Colonel Richardson Middle School — meet the criteria and have district coordinators assigned to them.
Supervisor of Student Services Nicole Fisher reported the Pillar 4 team is committed to evidence-based practices, but challenges facing the district are providing adequate behavioral health staffing and transportation.
Simmons said "As Blueprint ratchets up, all nine of our schools are going to qualify for Concentration of Poverty funding due to the FARMS (Free and Reduced-Price Meals) rates in all of our schools … in about another two or three years."
Pillar 5: Governance and Accountability
"Pillar 5 is what pulls together all of the other pillars," Simmons said, explaining that the pillar focuses on governance and accountability.
Two main areas of focus are the "stakeholder engagement plan" and Blueprint funding and resources which require "money following the students."
"Pillars 1 through 4 have done an incredible job of reaching out to community members, and they've got strong, robust teams that are getting lots of feedback," Simmons said, elaborating on the stakeholder engagement objective.
"There are shifts — monumental shifts in some areas — for the way that we're doing (Blueprint)," he said. "But eventually we'll stop talking about Blueprint, and we'll just be talking about what it is that we're doing that connects to the strategic plan, because the overlap will be there when it's closer to full implementation."

title: Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding
author: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service
content:
Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 930
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore unveiled a budget proposal on Wednesday that would balance the books and protect the state's ambitious reform plan for Maryland public schools, without raising taxes in the fiscal year that begins in July.The $63.1 billion plan would balance the books where officials had projected a shortfall, in part by returning some programs to spending levels closer to those of the pre-pandemic era. The plan proposes leveraging state debt and dipping into rainy day funds.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's sweeping education plan of 2021, will be fully funded, state budget officials said Wednesday. Moore, a Democrat, said his administration crafted the budget plan in partnership with lawmakers, community leaders and other "village elders."
"We wanted to make sure that this proposed budget had everyone's fingerprints on it," Moore said in his public announcement of the new plan. "Because this budget is not just a reflection of an administration. This budget is a reflection of our shared aspiration."
Those aspirations will now go to the Maryland General Assembly for debate. Lawmakers have set a target of early April for passing a budget, and the state Constitution requires that it be balanced.
But the joint Republican Caucus will look closely at where funding transfers in the proposed budget are coming from, House Minority Leader Jason Buckel, R-Allegany, told Capital News Service.
While he said he is pleased that the Moore administration kept total spending similar to that of years past, he expressed concerns about the possibility of fees for certain businesses or tax hikes down the road. Buckel said he'll keep worrying about that possibility until the legislature adjourns.
"All in all, it's a mixed bag, I think, and we'll look forward to working with the governor and working with the Democratic leadership here to try to make the budget as good as possible," Buckel said.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey suggested he worries about the possibility of fee increases down the road.
"While it is a relief that the governor's budget spends less than last year and does not raise taxes, the number of fee increases proposed by his administration through legislation and the regulatory process is concerning," said Hershey, a Republican representing Kent, Cecil, Queen Anne's and Caroline, in an email release. He and other Republicans contend fee hikes are coming through the administrative pipeline.
"Taxes aren't the only way to raise revenue," Hershey said, "and state government should not be in the business of nickel and diming Maryland's families and small businesses."
The only fee increases currently in the budget plan are in the Department of the Environment, and those would generate roughly $3.5 million in revenue, according to a spokesman for the governor's office.
Working together to approve a balanced budget had been shaping up as no easy task. The state's spending had been projected to outpace revenues starting in the coming fiscal year, according to a recent report from the Department of Legislative Services.
But Moore has now proposed a plan that would instead balance the 2025 budget, saying it is a step in the right direction toward addressing the state's structural deficit in the years beyond that.
His budget flips the expected cash shortfall of $1.1 billion to a positive cash balance of $103 million in fiscal 2025, according to Helene Grady, Maryland's secretary of budget and management.
Moore said his budget prioritizes public safety, affordable housing, child care, education and public service. It also raises pay for state employees.
"We know that budgets, they're moral documents," Moore said. "Where we choose to invest actually defines our values. And it dictates the course of our future."
State budget officials said they avoided wide-ranging cuts across the board, hiring freezes or salary freezes. Rather, state agency heads went through an intense process and found areas to trim, and several agency budgets will be lower this year than they were the year before.
Moore said he proposed a record $127 million for local police agencies, citing the importance of supporting law enforcement and getting "more boots on the ground" to solve crimes and keep repeat offenders off the streets. Other investments would go toward the prevention of gun violence and support for crime victims.
While addressing public safety, Moore acknowledged the debates about juvenile justice likely to come during the legislative session, announcing an increase in funding to the Department of Juvenile Services. He didn't specifically discuss any cuts made to juvenile services programs.
Affordable housing and child care would receive significant funding under the proposal. Those are two areas Moore claimed are the biggest strains on Maryland residents. Access to housing and child care allow for increased participation in the workforce as Maryland tries to grow its economy, he argued.
"Access to child care doesn't just affect your child and your family," Moore said. "It changes the trajectory of our state's fiscal health."
Options for job training in innovative industries and public service were a priority. Through Moore's budget, the state is on track to increase the number of Service Year Option and Maryland Corps participants to 500, as required by law.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future will be fully funded in the coming fiscal year, budget officials said, but its money problems are far from resolved. Prior to the beginning of the legislative session, the Department of Legislative Services report projected the state would exhaust the Blueprint balance in fiscal 2027.
"It's not inaccurate to say, 'Hey, we funded the Blueprint, or at least the state's portion of the Blueprint, for today,'" Buckel said. "But I also think it's completely honest to say the blueprint looming large over the next four or five years, blows billion-dollar holes into our state budget."

title: Talbot Board of Education discusses proposed budget, Blueprint's affects
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Talbot Board of Education discusses proposed budget, Blueprint's affects

 January 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 621
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — At a Talbot County Board of Education meeting Wednesday, Talbot County Public Schools Superintendent Sharon Pepukayi and Chief Financial Officer Sarah Jones went over the proposed fiscal year 2025 budget.At the beginning of their presentation, Pepukayi shared the Board of Education and superintendent priorities. These priorities are to improve economic equity and achievement in math; foster an engaging environment for students and staff; recruit, promote and retain staff and meet the the Blueprint for Maryland's Future objectives.
The Blueprint is a plan, passed by the Maryland General Assembly in 2021, that aims to improve student outcomes and the quality of education across the state through increasing education funding by $3.8 billion each year over the next 10 years.
Talbot County Public Schools' current draft fiscal year 2025 budget is $80.03 million. According to the presentation, the proposed budget is $7.98 million more than that of the fiscal year prior.
After Pepukayi spoke, Jones listed where those increases to the budget come from. These include the addition of 16 positions and money set aside to achieve a $60,000 starting salary for teachers by fiscal year 2027, a Blueprint requirement aimed at attracting and retaining high quality and diverse teachers.
The district's budget increase in technology devices and software costs is due to the expiration of COVID-19-related grants. Jones said a significant amount of annual technology costs had come out of grant money over the past few years.
"Those grants are expiring," she said. "So that translates to an increase in our request for FY25."
Another reason for the budget increase is the district's community school initiatives for next year.
According to the Maryland State Department of Education, community schools work with community partners, local governments and other stakeholders "to identify and address structural and institutional barriers to achievement." These schools receive Concentration of Poverty Grants, which give schools startup funding and per-pupil dollars to sustain them.
Jones said Easton Middle School will be coming on as a new community school and that Easton Elementary School is in its third year as a community school. She said the cost increases for these initiatives are mainly payroll related.
Jones said there are two potential reductions that could be made to the proposed budget that would save about $259,000 "without impacting student learning."
The first possible reduction would be to bring down the budget line for dual enrollment. Jones said the district realized, after getting the bill from Chesapeake College, that it had overestimated costs — particularly for instruction materials.
The second possible reduction would be to pay over time for a new school bus the district intends to buy, rather than paying for the bus in full.
After the presentation, Board President Emily Jackson asked if it was possible for the district to quantify how much of that $7.98 million increase directly applies to the Blueprint.
"I want to make sure we are telling our story in a way that is effective to the people who have to go and approve the budget and understand why we are asking for this much more money," she said.
Jones said Jackson's ask is a challenge because the Blueprint is "so embedded in what we're doing" that it's hard to differentiate which costs are tied to the Blueprint and which aren't. But, she said that, of the 16 new positions, she could say which were specifically tied to the Blueprint.
Board Vice President Candace Henry said past cuts to the budget could speak to the Blueprint's affect on the proposed fiscal year 2025 budget.
"We could speak to things that we've had to cut out of previous years, and now — because of Blueprint — we have to have," she said. "So I think we can use some of that information to tell that story to the public as well."

title: Superintendent shares schools' budget constraints with Commissioners
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Superintendent shares schools' budget constraints with Commissioners

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline County Public Schools officials shared good news and bad news with the Caroline County Commissioners at a Jan. 16 meeting.The good news: Caroline County Public Schools ended the year with a $3.25 million surplus.
The not-so-good news: The Blueprint for Maryland's Future unfunded mandate puts the fiscal squeeze on the budget and pandemic-based grant funding disappears in fiscal year 2025, officials said.
Chief Finance Officer Erin Thornton and Superintendent Dr. Derek Simmons shared with the commissioners what they need to prepare for as the school district's budget planning continues.
"We have always been good stewards of the money and we're fiscally conservative, trying not to just spend money just to spend it, so we were prepared to end the year with money on the books," Thornton said.
The unassigned fund balance is currently at $9.5 million, "which is approximately 8.4% of our current operating budget," she said. "Our target range for a fund balance is one to 10%. So, we are approaching a high, which is where we want to be."
Commissioner Frank Bartz asked about maintaining support services salaries, something that he said is not addressed in the Blueprint.
"A lot of people in the county work for support services," he said. "I just want to make sure that they're taken care of."
"You're spot on," Simmons said. "The Blueprint addresses teachers only and leaves out two-thirds of our workgroup, and (it) does not take into consideration any support staff or administration. Required increases to salaries are … for the most part, to classroom-based teachers with kids on the workload."
Simmons said the Supportive Services Association is a negotiated employee group.
"Their contract was ratified to be closed from 2012 until next year, so that has been a closed contract with a required 1% in step every year, and then it's 1% in addition to whatever the teachers get. Their contract comes open next year for us to negotiate."
Simmons said the "biggest challenge that we're going to see this year" is the Blueprint formula's increase of 1.7% over last year's budget "when inflation is currently still running over 3%, and that factors in no increases in health insurance, which is probably 5% to 7% right now, we're hearing."
That percentage does not factor in any pay increase. Blueprint requires first-year classroom teachers to be earning $60,000 by fiscal year 2027.
"After this year, the budget increases roughly 5%," Simmons said. "We're sitting in a different position in our county than some of our colleagues are in others. … A lot of the larger systems are looking at significant cuts of teaching positions because (of) that 1.7% increase. It's a regressive budget no matter how you cut it, when it's only that much of an increase, and the cost of living is definitely a lot higher."
When COVID funding and (Maryland) Leads funding "dries up in September at the same time as we're getting a 1.7% increase, that's the perfect storm," Simmons said. "And again, we'll weather it for our staff. We'll figure it out. I really, truly believe we will. It's just going to be a really tough year."

title: DCPS presentations show improvements in the district
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
DCPS presentations show improvements in the district

 January 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 405
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Kindergarten readiness among Dorchester County kindergarteners is up 7% from last school year.This was one of multiple data points shared during a Dorchester County Board of Education meeting Jan. 18 that show improvements among Dorchester County Public Schools.
Jodi Colman, DCPS director of curriculum, instruction and assessment, gave a presentation on the most recent Kindergarten Readiness Assessment results.
Assessment results are broken down into three sections: demonstrating readiness, approaching readiness and emerging readiness.
According to Colman's presentation, a student who is demonstrating kindergarten readiness "has most of the foundational skills and behaviors necessary for kindergarten." A student who is approaching readiness has some of those foundational skills and behaviors. A student who is emerging readiness has few of those foundational skills and behaviors.
The percent of kindergarteners demonstrating readiness went up to 39% this school year from 32% last school year. The year before that, in the 2021-2022 school year, 29% of students were demonstrating kindergarten readiness.
"I wish I had some confetti and a little horn to celebrate," Colman said about this year's results.
Although the percentage of students demonstrating readiness went up this school year, so did the percentage of students emerging readiness. It was at 38% this school year compared to 30% last year.
The percentage of students approaching readiness decreased to 33% this school year from 38% last school year.
The district saw an increase in the number of its kindergarteners demonstrating readiness in language and literacy and mathematics, but it saw a decrease in its kindergarteners demonstrating readiness in social foundations and physical well-being and motor development.
"I do think that speaks to the level of need for some of our students in the younger grades and the mental health supports that they need, the social development that they need," Colman said. "Those are our COVID babies and I think that kind of hit us here."
STAR RATINGS
Colman also presented on the different star ratings for each school in the district. Star ratings are given by the state and determined by different academic and school quality indicators.
According to Colman's presentation, every school except for Vienna Elementary School kept it's star rating from the year before. Vienna Elementary went down from four stars in the 2021-2022 school year to three stars in the 2022-2023 school year.
Colman said three DCPS schools that were less than one percentage point away from gaining another star. Those schools were Mace's Lane Middle School, Sandy Hill Elementary School and North Dorchester Middle School.

title: Eastern Shore Delegation to ask governor for Cade formula restoration
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Eastern Shore Delegation to ask governor for Cade formula restoration

 January 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: General Assembly 
 
 482
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — At a meeting Friday, the Eastern Shore Delegation voted to send a letter to the governor's office asking that the Cade Funding Formula for community colleges be restored in a supplemental budget.Gov. Wes Moore's proposed fiscal year 2025 budget calls for the reduction of $22 million in Cade formula funding to community colleges in the state.
The Cade formula essentially ties state funding for community colleges to state funding for designated University System of Maryland institutions, according to the Maryland Association of Community Colleges.
Moore's proposal would reduce the Cade formula from 29% to 26.5%.
That percentage — the amount of funding community colleges receive from the state — is based on the funding given to public four-year institutions per full-time equivalent student.
At the Eastern Shore Delegation meeting, legislators were joined by the presidents of colleges that are located on the Eastern Shore, as well as MACC Executive Director Brad Phillips.
Phillips called rebasing the Cade formula a "budget word" for inequity.
"Look at it this way," he said. "If you're giving a student a dollar to go to a University System of Maryland or a four-year public institution, the policy goal is that 29 cents goes to community colleges. ... (with the reduction,) you're cutting community colleges out. You're still providing a dollar to our four-year friends."
Wor-Wic Community College President Deborah Casey told the delegation she had spent hours preparing a budget with an 11% cut.
"That's $1.5 million for Wor-Wic Community College," she said of the budget cut. "That doesn't work for us."
Casey said that she can't build infrastructure and carry Wor-Wic in the best direction with a budget reduction of this magnitude.
"And you're expecting and asking us, and holding us accountable to making sure we're meeting many needs of this community," she said. "Please help us get that full funding."
Phillips said Maryland's community colleges are up 8.3% in enrollment this year.
"So this is a cut that would actually stretch less funding to more students," he said.
During the meeting, both Casey and Chesapeake College President Cliff Coppersmith mentioned increases in enrollment at their schools.
Del. Sheree Sample-Hughes (D-Dorchester, Wicomico) said this increased enrollment is one reason why this formula change is concerning.
Del. Jefferson Ghrist (R-36, Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), who made the motion to send the letter, said the Maryland Department of Legislative Services had given the House Appropriations Committee, which he is a member of, a list of possible cuts that could be made in order to restore the Cade formula to 29%.
"There's a lot of places that we can go to find money to restore that," he said.
Ghrist said getting the Cade formula restored in a supplemental budget, however, would make the job of the House Appropriations Committee easier.
"That way it'll be done before we start really getting down to work on the budget," he said. "That would make our jobs a heck of a lot easier on the committee."
